entries.title: Four core functions
entries.text: NIST structures its AI Risk Management Framework around four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. Govern spans the lifecycle; the other functions help establish context, assess risks and determine responses.
entries.keywords: core four functions govern map measure manage lifecycle

entries.title: Status and intended users
entries.text: NIST AI RMF 1.0 is voluntary guidance for organisations designing, developing, deploying or using AI systems. It offers a common approach to managing risks, not an automatic compliance certification.
entries.keywords: voluntary nonbinding guidance organisation compliance certification

entries.title: Governance roles and accountability
entries.text: The Govern function concerns organisational policies, risk management culture, clear roles and responsibilities, documented practices and oversight across the AI lifecycle.
entries.keywords: govern leadership accountability roles responsibilities oversight policies

entries.title: Context before measurement
entries.text: The Map function asks teams to identify the AI system's purpose, context, intended uses, affected people and plausible impacts before treating risks as measurable technical scores.
entries.keywords: map context purpose intended use stakeholders people impacts

entries.title: Assess and monitor risks
entries.text: The Measure function uses quantitative and qualitative approaches to analyse, assess, benchmark and monitor identified AI risks, including uncertainty and limitations of available measures.
entries.keywords: measure testing evaluation monitoring metrics qualitative quantitative uncertainty

entries.title: Prioritise risk responses
entries.text: The Manage function turns mapped and measured risks into prioritised responses, decisions on treatment and monitoring across the AI system lifecycle.
entries.keywords: manage prioritize prioritise mitigation response incident operations

entries.title: Trustworthy AI characteristics
entries.text: NIST's trustworthy-AI characteristics include validity and reliability, safety, security and resilience, accountability and transparency, explainability and interpretability, privacy, and fairness with harmful bias managed.
entries.keywords: trustworthy fairness reliability safety privacy bias explainability security

entries.title: Generative-AI-specific risks
entries.text: The Generative AI Profile examines risks such as fabricated or misleading content (confabulation), harmful or biased outputs, information-integrity concerns, privacy exposure and misuse. It supplements rather than replaces the AI RMF.
entries.keywords: hallucinations confabulation misinformation fabricated content bias privacy genai

entries.title: Pre-deployment evaluation
entries.text: For generative AI systems, evaluation needs to be matched to intended use and harmful failure modes; testing can examine validity, safety, resilience and the tendency to produce unsupported claims before deployment.
entries.keywords: predeployment test benchmark evaluate generation answers claims safety

entries.title: Post-deployment monitoring
entries.text: Generative AI risk management does not end at launch: teams should monitor use and incidents, revisit evaluations and update controls as systems, contexts and threats change.
entries.keywords: monitor drift incidents postdeployment operations controls

entries.title: Provenance and transparency
entries.text: Generative-AI governance benefits from documenting data provenance, model limitations and how content is produced or used, so downstream users can assess reliability and possible harms.
entries.keywords: training data provenance documentation limits transparency sources

entries.title: Human rights and democratic values
entries.text: The OECD Principles call for AI to respect the rule of law, human rights and democratic values, including fairness, privacy and the ability of people to challenge inappropriate outcomes.
entries.keywords: rights fairness democracy privacy challenge contest decisions

entries.title: Transparency and explainability
entries.text: The OECD calls on AI actors to provide meaningful information about AI systems where appropriate, so people can understand their interactions and, when adversely affected, challenge outcomes.
entries.keywords: disclosure explainability transparency explanation notice users

entries.title: Robustness, security and safety
entries.text: The OECD Principles emphasise that AI systems should function appropriately under reasonably foreseeable use and misuse, with safeguards for robustness, security and safety throughout their lifecycle.
entries.keywords: robustness security safety misuse resilience

entries.title: Accountability and traceability
entries.text: The OECD holds AI actors accountable for proper functioning of AI systems in line with their roles and context, and emphasises traceability, risk management and continuing assessment.
entries.keywords: accountability traceability responsible actors audit monitoring

entries.title: Workers and social transition
entries.text: OECD recommendations encourage governments to prepare people for transformations in work and to promote a fair transition as AI changes tasks and labour markets.
entries.keywords: jobs labour workers employment training workforce transition

entries.title: Ethical impact assessments
entries.text: UNESCO recommends ethical impact assessments that examine potential effects of AI on human rights, communities, society and the environment, with attention to different groups and contexts.
entries.keywords: ethical impact assessment rights assessment affected groups

entries.title: Data governance and privacy
entries.text: UNESCO's policy areas address data policy and governance, privacy, data quality, access and safeguards against harmful uses of personal information.
entries.keywords: data governance privacy consent personal information

entries.title: Gender, inclusion and inequality
entries.text: UNESCO calls for attention to gender equality, non-discrimination, social inclusion and groups at greater risk of being excluded or harmed by AI systems.
entries.keywords: gender inclusion marginalized equality discrimination bias

entries.title: Environmental implications
entries.text: UNESCO treats environmental and ecosystem impacts as a dedicated AI policy area, asking policymakers to consider both potential benefits and ecological costs.
entries.keywords: environment ecology carbon energy ecosystems

entries.title: Human oversight and accountability
entries.text: UNESCO emphasises human oversight, transparency, responsibility and mechanisms for monitoring the ethical effects of AI systems; automation does not remove human responsibility.
entries.keywords: human oversight accountability governance responsibility audit

entries.title: Research and capacity-building
entries.text: UNESCO highlights education, research, international cooperation and capacity development, including attention to countries facing unequal access to resources and expertise.
entries.keywords: training research development capacity global south inequality

entries.title: Risk-based legal approach
entries.text: The European Union AI Act uses a risk-based structure: some AI uses are prohibited, high-risk uses face stronger requirements, and certain other AI uses face transparency obligations. It does not treat all systems alike.
entries.keywords: risk based categories prohibited high risk transparency low risk

entries.title: High-risk application areas
entries.text: The European Commission identifies high-risk AI use cases in sensitive fields such as employment, education, essential services, migration and border control, as well as certain regulated products. Classification depends on the actual intended use.
entries.keywords: employment hiring migration border education essential services high risk

entries.title: Controls for high-risk AI
entries.text: The AI Act sets obligations for relevant high-risk systems covering risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency for deployers, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity.
entries.keywords: high risk documentation logging oversight accuracy cybersecurity governance

entries.title: Transparency obligations
entries.text: The EU framework includes transparency duties for certain AI interactions and synthetic content. Which duty applies depends on the system and use case; this overview is not a substitute for legal advice.
entries.keywords: chatbot disclosure deepfake synthetic content transparency

entries.title: Regulatory timelines change
entries.text: EU AI Act implementation dates and transitional arrangements can be amended. Before making a compliance decision, review the current regulation and European Commission guidance rather than relying on a static portfolio example.
entries.keywords: dates deadlines timeline implementation compliance updates
